source.title: RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training

atoms.canonical_statement: The study asks how multi-turn agentic RL can be stabilized by jointly addressing rollout–training consistency, turn-level credit assignment, and asynchronous policy drift.
The authors model multi-turn interaction as a hierarchical Markov decision process with turn-level states defined by interaction history and turn-level actions defined by complete model responses.
The standard flattened PPO/GRPO-style objective assigns one trajectory-level advantage uniformly to unmasked tokens across the full interaction trajectory.

When rollout uses a truncated or summarized context but training recomputes likelihoods on the full flattened history, the importance-sampling denominator no longer matches the distribution that sampled the token.
The theoretical analysis identifies non-injective context compression as a potential source of state aliasing that can restrict optimization to an observation-induced policy class.

The trajectory-level advantage is decomposed into downstream stochasticity, the true turn advantage, and an upstream state effect, showing why a single trajectory reward can misattribute credit at a turn.
The authors show that independently clipping token-level importance ratios is not equivalent to correcting the full-trajectory importance ratio, with discrepancy compounding over long trajectories.
RTPO represents a K-turn episode as a turn-boundary MDP whose per-turn conditioning context is exactly the context observed by the model at rollout time.

RTPO records the exact rollout conditioning context and old-policy log probabilities, then uses the same conditioning context during training while applying loss only to the current turn output tokens.
RTPO trains turns in temporal reverse order from K−1 to 0 so that downstream turn policies have already been optimized and are held fixed when an earlier turn is updated.
At each reverse phase, RTPO restores the trunk trajectory boundary state and generates G−1 sibling continuations from that same state to obtain a state-matched group-relative turn advantage.
Only sibling rollouts contribute gradient updates at a turn; the trunk trajectory is retained as a state anchor and receives no gradient.

Theorem 1 states that reverse-order turn-level optimization converges to recursive optimality under finite state/action spaces, Robbins–Monro step sizes, sufficient per-turn exploration, frozen downstream policies, and bounded rewards; global optimality additionally requires complete macro-action spaces.
RTPO estimates a turn-level advantage by comparing sibling terminal returns from the same boundary state, removing the upstream state-contamination term from cross-state trajectory comparisons.

RTPO uses a MAXQ-style decomposition in which the turn action value combines local reward and the discounted downstream continuation value; sibling terminal return serves as a Monte Carlo sample of that quantity.
Theorem 2 characterizes the sibling estimator as locally unbiased up to a finite-group multiplicative factor while eliminating upstream state contamination by holding the boundary state fixed.
Before each reverse-stage sibling generation, RTPO synchronizes the current downstream parameters to the inference engine and continues siblings to termination under that same policy.
Theorem 3 states that this on-policy continuation makes the full downstream trajectory importance weight identically one and reduces continuation-value error as downstream policies improve.

The main experiments use Qwen3-8B with thinking mode enabled for multi-turn agentic RL rollouts and compare RTPO with GRPO, ARPO, TreeGRPO, and SeeUPO across mathematical and knowledge-reasoning tasks.
The main evaluation covers eight benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning and knowledge-intensive question answering and reports accuracy together with tool-call behavior.
All methods are implemented in VeRL, with vLLM used for rollout generation and FSDP for distributed training.
The experiments include controlled analyses for rollout–training consistency, turn-level credit assignment, and on-policy versus off-policy continuation in addition to end-task performance.

The training setup uses a global sampling budget of 80,000 rollouts for mathematical reasoning and 16,000 for knowledge reasoning, with the authors stating that RTPO does not exceed baseline aggregate rollout compute.
The maximum interaction horizon is three turns for mathematical reasoning and six turns for web search; RTPO uses two sibling rollouts per realized boundary in the default G=3 configuration.
The authors report repeating each experiment three times and averaging performance to mitigate randomness.
The authors state that RTPO source code is provided in the supplementary material with installation instructions, versioned dependencies, and training/evaluation scripts.
For Qwen3 multi-turn context management, prior <think> content is removed before the next turn while commentary, tool call, and tool result are retained as the visible conditioning context.

Algorithm 1 separates RTPO into a trunk-rollout phase followed by reverse-order per-turn synchronization, on-policy sibling generation, group-advantage computation, and PPO updates over only current-turn tokens.
RTPO achieved 33.33% Pass@1 on AIME24.
RTPO achieved 26.67% Pass@1 on AIME25.
RTPO achieved 67.50% Pass@1 on AMC23.
RTPO achieved 86.20% Pass@1 on MATH500.
RTPO achieved 94.84% Pass@1 on GSM8K.
RTPO achieved 55.49% Pass@1 on OE-Math.
RTPO achieved 64.89% best-span F1 on HotpotQA.
RTPO achieved 64.35% best-span F1 on 2Wiki.
Across the eight main benchmarks, RTPO achieved an overall accuracy score of 61.66.
The paper reports RTPO improved overall accuracy by 21.50% relative to GRPO.
The paper reports RTPO improved overall accuracy by 10.76% relative to SeeUPO.
The paper reports RTPO improved overall accuracy by 66.78% relative to the untuned vanilla model.
Under the controlled full-history credit-assignment setting, RTPO-CA achieved overall Pass@1 of 79.13 across four mathematical benchmarks.

atoms.canonical_statement: The appendix reports RTPO HotpotQA performance as 64.89±0.34 over three evaluation runs.
On the held-out 20-task τ3-Airline test set, RTPO (G=3) achieved Pass@1 of 17.50%.
On the held-out 20-task τ3-Airline test set, RTPO (G=3) achieved Pass@4 of 30.00%.
On held-out τ3-Airline tasks, RTPO executed 74 of 83 attempted tool calls successfully, for an execution-success rate of 89.16%.
Increasing the sibling group from G=3 to G=4 increased τ3-Airline Pass@1 from 17.50% to 20.00%.
Increasing the sibling group from G=3 to G=4 reduced the zero-advantage rate from 89.61% to 82.66%.
Increasing the sibling group from G=3 to G=4 raised training GPU-hours from 21.48 to 28.06 and training-generation tokens from 846,207 to 2,139,039.
Under the same Qwen3-1.7B hardware setting, RTPO (G=3) used 21.48 GPU-hours versus 15.20 for GRPO, an approximately 41.3% increase.
In the compute-matched τ3-Airline comparison, RTPO achieved Pass@4 of 35.00% versus 25.00% for GRPO while using 15.55 versus 15.20 GPU-hours.
Under the matched maximum inference budget, RTPO achieved 0.104 successful trajectories per 1,000 response tokens, compared with 0.046 for GRPO and 0.064 for Tree-GRPO.

population.label: τ3-Airline held-out test tasks under matched inference budget

atoms.canonical_statement: During τ3-Airline online training, RTPO success peaked at 56.25% at Step 40 and then fell to 40.63% at Step 50.

RTPO depends on the quality of the sampled trunk because sibling branches are anchored to states visited by that trunk; poor early trunk decisions can yield low-value later states and near-zero turn advantages.
Reverse multi-turn training adds cost that scales with the number of turns and sibling rollouts and requires repeated inference-engine synchronization for on-policy continuation.
RTPO intentionally applies gradients only to current-turn sibling tokens, leaving prefix, downstream-continuation, and trunk tokens unused for the PPO loss, which reduces training-token utilization.

The strict convergence guarantee is for a turn-level tabular formulation with exactly fixed downstream policies; a shared neural policy only approximates that structure and does not inherit a global non-convex convergence guarantee.
Even with G=4, the zero-advantage rate in the sparse binary-reward τ3-Airline environment remains above 80%, indicating a sparse and inefficient learning signal.
The τ3-Airline online success rate declines from 56.25% at Step 40 to 40.63% at Step 50, which the authors identify as possible late-stage over-optimization on a limited sparse-reward training set.

The reported experiments are limited to three-run averages, Qwen3-4B/8B in the original experiments plus Qwen3-1.7B in supplementary evaluation, and turn horizons of three for math and six for web search; broader scales, seeds, horizons, and synchronization schedules remain untested.

The authors caution that stronger long-horizon agents may produce confident errors, misuse tools, or amplify harmful automation and recommend safety constraints, tool-use monitoring, privacy-preserving data handling, and human oversight for deployment.
The authors conclude that RTPO unifies rollout–training consistency, turn-level credit assignment, and on-policy continuation into a more stable training framework for long-horizon tool-using agents.
